title: Cancellation is part of an async contract
paragraphs: A cancellation token is not an emergency stop button. It is a request that each operation must observe at a safe point, particularly before starting expensive I/O.
Pass the caller's token through to database and HTTP calls, and let cancellation propagate instead of turning it into a misleading success response.

title: Deadlines for slow HTTP calls
paragraphs: An HTTP request without a deadline can occupy resources long after its caller has stopped waiting. Choose a timeout based on the experience your application can offer, not just the server's usual latency.
Combine the deadline with caller cancellation and distinguish a timeout from an intentional cancellation in your logs.

title: Bounded parallelism beats a thousand tasks
paragraphs: Starting one task per item looks concise until a large batch opens too many connections. A small concurrency limit protects the remote service and keeps memory usage predictable.
Measure throughput at several limits. The fastest local run is not necessarily the best setting when many application instances share the same dependency.

title: Tracing an async request across services
paragraphs: A request may cross a queue, an API and a database before it returns. A trace connects those steps so that a slow response can be investigated as one journey.
Keep span names stable and useful, and avoid attaching secrets or unbounded user input to attributes.

title: Retrying asynchronous work without duplicates
paragraphs: A failed response does not always mean the server failed to process a request. Retrying a payment or a message blindly can repeat the side effect.
Use an idempotency key where the operation supports one, and retry only failures that are likely to be temporary.

title: Streaming records with async enumeration
paragraphs: An async stream lets a consumer process records as they arrive instead of waiting for a complete collection. That can reduce peak memory for large exports.
Streaming is not free: the underlying connection may remain open while the consumer works, so cancellation and disposal still matter.

title: Reading a database index like a map
paragraphs: A database index helps locate rows without reading the whole table, but each additional index also has a cost when rows change.
Start with an actual query and its execution plan. Choose columns based on filtering and ordering rather than adding an index to every field.

title: Column order in a composite index
paragraphs: A composite index on category and publish date can help a query that filters by category and orders by date. Reversing the columns changes which access patterns it supports efficiently.
Look at the real filters, sort order and data distribution before deciding. A plausible index name is not evidence that the optimizer uses it.

title: Offset and cursor pagination in a blog archive
paragraphs: Offset pagination is easy to understand and works well for small archives, but large offsets can require the database to walk past many rows.
Cursor pagination uses the last visible sort key. Include a unique tie breaker with the publish date so that posts sharing a timestamp are not skipped.

title: Keeping a transaction small
paragraphs: A transaction should protect the changes that must succeed together, not the entire request including a slow network call.
Keep the critical section short and decide what happens when the process crashes after committing but before notifying another service.

title: When a query plan changes after launch
paragraphs: A query that was fast with a tiny development database may behave differently after months of production data. Skewed values and stale statistics can change the optimizer's choices.
Capture the slow query and compare plans before applying a fix. Measure the effect on both reads and writes.

title: The missing value is not an empty string
paragraphs: A null value and an empty string can mean different things: unknown is not the same as deliberately blank. Mixing them makes filters and reports harder to explain.
Write the rule into the data model and test comparisons explicitly, especially when data enters through more than one application.

title: Why search splits a phrase into tokens
paragraphs: A search index usually stores terms produced by an analyzer rather than the original sentence alone. Case folding and punctuation rules decide which words become searchable.
Inspect the analyzer before tuning relevance. A query for an exact phrase and a query for any matching word may need different behavior.

title: Should a title match outrank a body match?
paragraphs: A title often summarizes the subject of a post, while a word in the body might only be a passing reference. Giving title matches extra weight can make results feel more useful.
Collect representative searches before changing scores. A boost that helps one query can hide a valuable article for another.

title: Searching tags alongside article text
paragraphs: Tags provide an editorial signal that can complement full-text search. A post tagged database may be relevant even when its title uses the word SQL instead.
Normalize the tag vocabulary and decide whether a tag match should be treated as a filter, a ranking signal, or both.

title: Finding similar posts without identical titles
paragraphs: Related articles should share a topic without simply repeating the current title. Tags and distinctive terms provide useful clues, but very common words can overwhelm the comparison.
Exclude the current post, inspect several neighborhoods of results, and compare the suggestions against posts on unrelated subjects.

title: Designing a useful empty search result
paragraphs: No results is still a result. Show the query, explain that nothing matched, and offer a way to revise the terms without losing the user's work.
Avoid implying that the index is broken when the query simply has no match. A clear empty state can make experimentation feel safe.

title: Rebuilding a search index after an import
paragraphs: Publishing content and finding it in search are related but separate events. Indexing may lag behind the database or fail for an individual document.
Before rebuilding everything, check indexing status and inspect a known post. A small diagnostic query can distinguish missing data from a broken analyzer.

title: A small vocabulary for useful blog tags
paragraphs: A tag list becomes difficult to navigate when every author invents a slightly different spelling. Decide which concepts deserve a shared label and keep the labels understandable.
A small controlled vocabulary can grow over time. Review near-duplicates before merging them, because similar words may represent distinct topics.

title: Counting posts for a tag overview
paragraphs: A tag overview can show readers where a blog has depth, but its counts should match the content they are allowed to see.
Count published posts rather than drafts, define how casing is handled, and order labels consistently when two tags have the same count.

title: When tags should stay flat
paragraphs: A hierarchy can be useful for a large taxonomy, but many small blogs work better with a flat list of tags. Readers do not have to guess which branch contains a topic.
Start with clear names and add structure only when real navigation problems justify the extra editorial work.

title: Making a tag page worth visiting
paragraphs: A tag page is more than a database filter. A short description can explain what the topic includes and help visitors choose between neighboring tags.
List posts in a predictable order and make the empty state useful when an editor removes the last published article.

title: Renaming a tag without losing its readers
paragraphs: Changing a label can affect bookmarked URLs as well as the text shown in an editor. Treat a rename as a small content migration rather than a cosmetic edit.
Keep old links working where possible, and verify that counts and search results use the new vocabulary consistently.

title: Using shared tags as a similarity hint
paragraphs: Two articles sharing a specific tag are often related, but a broad tag like programming may be less informative than a narrower one.
Use tag overlap as one signal alongside titles and content. Test with articles that share one broad tag but otherwise discuss different subjects.

title: Composing an Umbraco article from blocks
paragraphs: A block list allows an editor to combine prose, code and other structured pieces in a single article. Each block has a clear job and can be rendered consistently.
Keep the available block types focused. Too many nearly identical choices make editing slower and make content harder to migrate.

title: Drafts and published content are different views
paragraphs: An editor may save a draft without changing what visitors see. Features that display public archives should use the published view rather than assuming every saved item is live.
Test updates, unpublishing and scheduled changes separately; each can change what belongs in a public listing.

title: Choosing fields for a blog post model
paragraphs: A title, editorial date, body and tags cover many blog use cases without making every field mandatory. Separate the date shown to readers from the time the database record was created.
Model additional fields only when an editor or a feature needs them. A smaller schema is easier to explain and maintain.

title: Importing content through CMS services
paragraphs: A content import needs more than database rows. The CMS must validate properties, maintain relationships and update its published view and search index.
Use supported content APIs, keep stable import identifiers, and make retries safe so an interrupted run does not create duplicates.

title: Building navigation from published pages
paragraphs: Navigation should reflect the structure readers can actually visit. A hidden or unpublished page may need different treatment from an ordinary child page.
Cache thoughtfully and invalidate when editors publish changes. Stale navigation can be more confusing than a slow initial render.

title: Testing a content preview before publishing
paragraphs: Preview lets an editor review a draft in its layout before visitors see it. It is especially useful for checking headings, long code samples and links.
Keep preview authorization separate from public rendering, and check that cached public responses never accidentally include draft content.

title: Caching an HTTP response responsibly
paragraphs: A cache can avoid repeated work, but only when the response is safe to share and its freshness rules are clear. Personalized content needs particular care.
Set explicit cache headers, test the behavior after publishing an update, and remember that a browser cache and a server cache are different layers.

title: Invalidating a cached blog archive
paragraphs: An archive may be inexpensive to cache until an editor publishes a new post. Without an invalidation strategy, readers can see an outdated list.
Choose between event-driven invalidation and a short lifetime based on how fresh the page must be and how reliably events reach every instance.

title: Preventing a cache stampede
paragraphs: When a popular cache entry expires, many requests can start the same expensive calculation at once. The result is a burst of load precisely when the cache was meant to help.
Coordinate refreshes where appropriate and consider serving a briefly stale value while one request rebuilds the entry.

title: Conditional requests with entity tags
paragraphs: An entity tag lets a client ask whether a representation has changed. If it has not, the server can avoid sending the same response body again.
Generate the tag from the actual representation or a reliable version, and check that all fields affecting the page are included in that version.

title: A practical guide to HTTP retry limits
paragraphs: A retry can recover from a brief network problem, but repeated requests can make an overloaded service struggle even more. Use a small limit and add backoff.
Check whether the operation is safe to repeat and respect a server's retry guidance. Always keep an overall deadline for the original request.

title: Choosing an HTTP status for a failed request
paragraphs: A status code gives clients a broad category for the outcome, while a response body can explain the specific problem. Avoid returning success for a request that failed validation.
Keep error details useful to the caller without exposing internal stack traces, credentials or other sensitive information.

title: Testing behavior at a service boundary
paragraphs: A focused test can describe how a service behaves when its dependency succeeds, fails or returns no data. The useful assertion is the observable outcome, not every internal method call.
Use a real implementation where practical and a fake for expensive or nondeterministic boundaries. Keep each example readable.

title: Making date-dependent tests predictable
paragraphs: A test that reads the current clock can fail around midnight or when it runs in another time zone. Control time explicitly when the behavior depends on it.
Include boundary cases such as a year change, and decide whether a publish date represents a local calendar day or an exact instant.

title: Search tests need more than one matching document
paragraphs: A single matching document proves little about ranking. Include close matches, partial matches and unrelated posts so a test can reveal surprising ordering.
For paging, create enough matches to cross a page boundary and check that adjacent pages do not repeat or silently omit results.

title: When a fake hides an integration bug
paragraphs: A fake database or content service can make a unit test fast, but it may not reproduce serialization, validation or transaction behavior.
Keep the focused unit tests and add a small integration test for the boundary where real infrastructure has important rules.

title: Testing pagination invariants
paragraphs: Paging logic has useful properties beyond one fixed example: every returned item belongs to the filtered set, ordering is stable, and neighboring pages should not overlap.
Exercise empty collections, exact page boundaries and duplicate sort values. A unique secondary key makes the expected order unambiguous.

title: Contract tests for a small JSON API
paragraphs: A JSON API contract includes field names, status codes and the meaning of optional values. A change to any of these can surprise a client even when the server compiles.
Test a few representative requests at the HTTP boundary and avoid coupling clients to undocumented implementation details.

title: Heading structure for readable articles
paragraphs: Headings describe the structure of an article, not just the size of its text. A clear sequence helps readers scan and helps assistive technology navigate between sections.
Choose heading levels based on the surrounding page and review the outline after composing blocks in the editor.

title: Writing link text that makes sense alone
paragraphs: A list of links labeled read more gives little information to someone navigating links out of context. Include the article title or another meaningful destination in the accessible name.
The visible text and the accessible name should agree so that speech input users can identify the control they want.

title: An accessible search form starts with a label
paragraphs: A placeholder disappears as soon as someone types and is not a substitute for a persistent label. Give the search field a clear name and a submit button that works with a keyboard.
After submission, make the result heading and any no-results message easy to find without relying only on color.

title: Making code examples easier to read
paragraphs: A code block should preserve whitespace and remain usable when a line is wider than the screen. Syntax colors need sufficient contrast and should not be the only way to distinguish meaning.
Include a short explanation before or after the example so that the code has context even when a reader skips it.

title: Visible focus in a keyboard journey
paragraphs: Keyboard users need to see which link or control will respond to the next action. Removing the browser's focus indicator without a replacement makes navigation much harder.
Test a complete journey through navigation, search and pagination rather than checking one isolated button.

title: Pagination controls with clear names
paragraphs: Page numbers need context: a link named only two is less helpful than one announced as page two. Mark the current page and keep previous and next actions predictable.
Check keyboard order and focus after a page change, especially if results update without a full navigation.

title: A mental model for the JavaScript event loop
paragraphs: JavaScript executes one piece of synchronous work at a time, while callbacks and promise continuations wait for an opportunity to run. Long synchronous tasks can delay user interaction.
Break large work into smaller pieces when responsiveness matters, and measure the actual delay in the browser rather than relying on assumptions.

title: Cancelling a stale browser search
paragraphs: When a reader types quickly, an earlier search request can finish after a later one and replace newer results. Abort the old request or ignore responses that are no longer current.
Handle intentional cancellation separately from a network failure so the interface does not show an error for normal typing.

title: Debouncing a search input
paragraphs: Debouncing waits for a pause in typing before issuing a search. It reduces unnecessary requests while keeping the interface responsive to the user's final query.
A debounce does not solve out-of-order responses on its own. Combine it with cancellation or a request sequence check.

title: Progressive enhancement for a search page
paragraphs: A plain form can submit a search query and display results without client-side code. JavaScript can then add conveniences such as suggestions or faster updates.
Keeping the basic flow functional makes the page more resilient to script failures and easier to use with a wider range of devices.

title: Keeping filters in the URL
paragraphs: A URL that includes the current query and page can be bookmarked, shared and revisited with the browser's back button. Hidden client state cannot offer the same affordance by itself.
Encode values using the platform URL APIs and define what happens when a parameter is missing or invalid.

title: Avoiding unnecessary DOM work
paragraphs: Updating a result list repeatedly inside a tight loop can create needless layout work. Prepare a batch of changes and apply it once when that makes the code clearer.
Measure before optimizing. Network latency, image size or server response time may matter more than the DOM operation you first noticed.

title: Logs that explain an import failure
paragraphs: An import log should identify the operation and the affected item without dumping article bodies or credentials. A clear summary helps an operator decide whether a retry is safe.
Record created, skipped and failed counts separately, and surface the original error with enough context to investigate it.

title: Choosing a useful latency metric
paragraphs: An average hides the experience of slow requests. Percentiles can reveal a long tail, especially when a dependency occasionally takes much longer than usual.
Compare measurements across similar workloads and include request volume. A percentile calculated from a handful of requests can be misleading.

title: Health checks and dependency failures
paragraphs: A process can be running while it is unable to serve useful requests. Separate a basic liveness check from readiness checks that consider essential dependencies.
Avoid making every optional integration a reason to restart a healthy application. Design the response around what the platform should do next.

title: A feature flag is not a cleanup plan
paragraphs: A feature flag can reduce deployment risk by allowing a change to be enabled separately from a release. It also introduces another branch that must be understood and tested.
Give temporary flags an owner and a removal condition. Otherwise old switches accumulate and make future changes harder to reason about.

title: Planning a reversible schema migration
paragraphs: A schema change can affect old and new application instances during a rolling deployment. Add compatible fields first and move data before removing the old representation.
Practice the migration on a representative copy and decide how to recover if an intermediate step fails.

title: A backup is only useful if it can be restored
paragraphs: A successful backup job does not prove that the resulting data can be restored. Test recovery into an isolated environment and check both the database and associated media.
Document the expected recovery steps and make sure the people responsible can perform them without relying on one developer's memory.

title: A small release checklist for a blog
paragraphs: Before releasing a blog change, check that an article renders, the archive lists it, and search can find it. These simple journeys cover several important integrations.
Keep the checklist short enough to use consistently, then automate repeatable checks where they provide reliable feedback.

title: A small workshop for evaluating search relevance
paragraphs: A relevance experiment starts with examples of what people are actually trying to find. Write down a handful of queries and the posts that would make useful answers, including a few queries that should return nothing.

Compare a title match with an article that discusses the same subject in its body. Include overlapping tags, broad programming terms and a deliberately unrelated post so that the test exposes both missed matches and false positives.

Run the same set after changing an analyzer or a field boost. Look at the first page and the next page, since a scoring improvement is not helpful if pagination repeats a result or hides a relevant document.

The goal is not to force every query into a predetermined order. Use the examples as a conversation starter, investigate surprising results and keep the dataset small enough that editors can understand it.
